warmup.text: Isaac's family is in the swamp now, with almost nothing. Watch how the people work together. Start with the warm-up sentence about Old Man and his blanket.

words.text: Today you build appositives yourself and use your roots to work out words you have never seen. The river game has root stones now. Tap only the letters of the root.

reading.text: Read Chapters 5 and 6. The photo on this tab shows a real cypress swamp in Mississippi. Look at the color of the water. Then reread one passage, the way What Good Readers Do asks.

assignment.text: Three questions, and then you revise. Add one inside detail to your draft: something you saw, heard, felt, or thought. One detail can change a whole paragraph.

do: Tap the highlighted words in the first sentence.
Fix the second sentence out loud.
Tap Check My Work to compare.
how.why: When the subject does the action, the sentence is clearer.

do: Find the root in each word.
Tap a word, then tap its meaning.
how.why: If you know the root, you can work out a word you have never seen.

do: Type the word that fits each sentence.
Open the Word Bank if you need it.
Tap Check My Words.
how.why: Putting a word back in its sentence shows you really know it.

do: Type the appositive in each sentence.
Tap Check My Work.
Combine the last two sentences in the box.
how.why: Building appositives yourself is how they end up in your own writing.

do: Say the word slowly.
Find where the first beat stops.
Tap the word, then its column.
how.why: Long words get easier when you split them into beats.

do: Pick a passage from Chapter 5 or 6.
Read it once for what happened.
Read it again for who is telling it.
how.why: Rereading shows you things you missed the first time.

do: Answer each question in 2 or more sentences.
Use details from Chapters 5 and 6.
how.why: These questions check how the people survive and what Isaac sees.

do: Reread your Day 2 draft.
Add one inside detail.
Write the new version in the box.
how.why: Revising means making your draft better, not starting over.
how.use: Next lesson you will write the final version.

glossary.meaning: what was happening around the story: the time, the place, and the events

nahullo: It names the men who came on horseback.
missionaries: People sent to teach their religion.
They were away visiting another town.
torches: Twenty of them fell from the sky.
smothering: Covering flames so they cannot burn.

miss.uniform: Say u-ni-form. The first beat, u, ends on the vowel u, and the u says its name. That makes it open.
miss.government: Say gov-ern-ment. The first beat, gov, ends on the consonant v, and the o is short. That makes it closed.
miss.station: Say sta-tion. The first beat, sta, ends on the vowel a, and the a says its name. That makes it open.
miss.territory: Say ter-ri-to-ry. The first beat, ter, ends on the consonant r, and the e is short. That makes it closed.
miss.frozen: Say fro-zen. The first beat, fro, ends on the vowel o, and the o says its name. That makes it open.
miss.mississippi: Say Mis-sis-sip-pi. The first beat, Mis, ends on the consonant s, and the i is short. That makes it closed.
miss.missionary: Say mis-sion-ar-y. The first beat, mis, ends on the consonant s, and the i is short. That makes it closed.
miss.wagon: Say wag-on. The first beat, wag, ends on the consonant g, and the a is short. That makes it closed.

game.title: Stones in the River
game.look: Each stone holds a word. Syllable stones: split the word after its first beat, then say open or closed. Root stones: tap only the letters of the root hiding inside the word. Every word you finish lights a stone, and your crossing keeps going all week.
game.doneLine: Every stone for today is lit.
game.sub: This week's word game · 6 stones today

do: Read the step under the river.
Syllable stone: tap the gap, then Open or Closed.
Root stone: tap the root's letters, then Check.
Tap Next stone.
how.why: Today's stones mix both of this week's skills: syllables and the roots mem and script.

stones.why: Yes: mem means memory. A memory is something you keep in your mind.
Yes. cab ends on the consonant b, and the vowel is short. Closed.
Yes: script means write. A postscript (P.S.) is written after the end of a letter.
Yes. pi ends on the vowel i, and it says its name. Open.
Yes: mem means memory. To remember is to bring something back to memory.
Yes: script means write. Scripture means sacred writings.

art.title: A cypress swamp in Mississippi
art.alt: Cypress trunks rising out of a swamp covered with bright green duckweed, lit by low sun.
art.look: This is a modern photo of a cypress swamp along the Natchez Trace Parkway in Mississippi, taken by the National Park Service in 2010. Look at the green water. Isaac says, “The swamp water was green and sticky.” Picture a hundred people making a home on an island in a place like this, with winter coming.
art.creator: National Park Service
